face: Southeast ridge, above the Crater Lake basin
overview: An alternate, less-traveled line up Raven Ridge's south side: approach via the Crater Creek Trail to Crater Lake, then climb the southeast ridge to an ~8,000 ft col before a short boulder scramble to the summit. Documented both as a summer scramble and as a January ski-mountaineering objective.
beta: From Crater Lake, ascend the southeast ridge directly to an approximately 8,000 ft col. Above treeline the terrain is boulder/talus, only lightly snow-covered even in winter conditions on the one documented ascent, requiring scrambling rather than just skinning to reach the summit. This is the quieter of Raven Ridge's two standard approaches (the other being the Libby Lake gully-ridge line to the north).
breakdown: Boulder scramble, SE col to summit: Class 2-3

first_pass.evidence: Crater Lake side reaches the same summit block, which goes at Class 3 via a short passage under the boulders; the ridge itself is Class 2-3.

overview: Rimrock Ridge is a remote, rarely climbed crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, mostly above 6,500 ft, forming the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek and running east and north-east from Old Guard Peak. Its high point lies a little over 3 miles north-east of Sentinel Peak. No trail reaches it: the few parties on record came onto its west end from the Ptarmigan Traverse near Sentinel Peak.
beta: No detailed route description exists for Rimrock Ridge. The recorded parties reached its west end from the Ptarmigan Traverse near Sentinel Peak and followed the crest east over its summits on cross-country alpine ground.

first_pass.evidence: Peakbagger lists Rimrock Ridge (7,254 ft) but no route description or rating was found anywhere; value is the record's own.

face: Northeast side, descending via the South Ridge-East Slope
overview: A cross-country mountaineering line up Rock Mountain's northeast side, reached by crossing the Howard-Rock col at the far end of a multi-summit Nason Ridge traverse (Mt. Mastiff - Mt. Howard - Rock Mountain), rather than via the maintained West Route trail.
beta: The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling), then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exit on the standard Rock Mountain Trail. Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).

first_pass.evidence: Only trip report describes the NE ridge from the Howard-Rock col as a snow climb and rock scramble, with no class given.

overview: A winter/spring line up Ruby's north side following the Happy Creek drainage — the least demanding way up the mountain in the right snow conditions.
beta: From the Happy Creek Nature Trail area on SR 20, leave the road just east of Happy Creek and climb its east side through forest, following (or starting on) the Happy Creek Nature Trail about 1.5 miles to a waterfall. Above the falls the bootpath steepens and grows fainter but stays followable, crossing a boulder field (snow-covered in the right season) before continuing up the north-side slopes to the summit.
breakdown: Highway/closure gate to Happy Creek Nature Trail split: Road walk/skin
Happy Creek Nature Trail to waterfall (~1.5 mi): Class 1, built trail
Above the waterfall to ~2,800 ft: Class 2, faint bootpath
~2,800 ft to summit (7,408 ft): Class 2-3, snow/scramble

first_pass.evidence: Winter route: short trail, then 5,000 ft of steep untracked forest and snow; finishes on the same summit ridge as the NW ridge (exposed rock and snow). No class given beyond 'winter scramble'.
first_pass.note: Snow route; top of the record's Class 2-3 range used.

overview: One of the most popular alpine rock routes at Washington Pass — the moderate, classic East Buttress of South Early Winter Spire. Enjoyable, well-featured climbing on excellent granite leads up the buttress to the summit.
beta: The specific route details are not well documented.

first_pass.evidence: No separate moderate 'East Buttress' route on SEWS found in MP's area list or other sources; only the Direct East Buttress (5.11a A0 / 5.9 A0) and South East Mank (5.7).

overview: A more technical, low-5th-class ridge scramble/climb on Sperry's south side - harder and more interesting than the standard route but without the commitment of the north/east face lines. It is heavily vegetated and not recommended for quality, though it is a real, documented line.
beta: Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge. The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengt

first_pass.evidence: Only trip-report mentions found (long day, poor-quality brushy rock); no source contradicts the record's 5.4 crux.

overview: A steep snow/ice line up a hook-shaped snow finger running direct to the summit on Spider Mountain's north face, first climbed by Dallas Kloke and Reed Tindall in 1972 and later established as a notable spring ski descent.
beta: The north face carries a prominent, gully-like snow/ice finger to the summit, guarded partway up by a large bergschrund. It is normally climbed (and, since 2003, skied) in winter or spring when the line is consolidated with neve/firm snow; conditions can include icy sections on the uppermost slope. By summer the face is reported to be bare, loose rock rather than a snow climb.

first_pass.evidence: North face is a narrow snow couloir, about 45+ deg at its steepest; no ice grade found (now mainly a ski descent).
first_pass.note: Steep snow with no ice grade mapped to Class 3.

face: South side of the summit ridge crest, reached via Point 5261
overview: A little-visited summit on the Cascade Crest near Stevens Pass, WA. Spinnaker Peak rises above the headwaters of the Tye River between Lichtenberg Mountain and Tye Peak, about a mile from the Pacific Crest Trail. It's rarely climbed, largely because the surrounding terrain is a thick, brushy bushwhack once snow melts out; most parties instead treat it as an off-trail winter or spring snow climb, often paired with neighboring Martin Peak.
beta: Two options exist to reach Spinnaker Peak's summit: the easier line climbs directly to the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak (steepest section of the trip, but low-exposure on the right line, and an ice axe isn't required if only Spinnaker is the objective); the harder option climbs Point 5261 first and follows the narrow, steeply-dropping ridge to Spinnaker's summit, which does require an ice axe and should be avoided in higher avalanche danger. first_pass.evidence: Via the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker: steepest part of the trip, minimal exposure; the ridge from Pt 5261 is narrow with steep drops. No class rating given.

overview: A rarely repeated technical line up Storm King's north face, first climbed in 1978 by Dick Emerson and Walt Grove. Unlike the walk-up-style Southwest Route, this is a genuine technical alpine rock climb, but little is known about its grade, pitch count, and exact line.
beta: Little is known beyond the first-ascent record: no pitch-by-pitch description, grade or length. Treat as an obscure, low-beta objective requiring independent route-finding on the north aspect of the peak.

first_pass.evidence: Only the existence of the 1978 Emerson-Grove North Face route was found (SummitPost/AAJ 1979 mention); no grade anywhere online, and the record has no grade column to fall back on.
first_pass.note: No final grade can be given without inventing one.

overview: Swiss Peak has no independently approached line — it is climbed as a link in Picket Range crest traverses. The most-documented ascent gains the West Fury–Swiss col over a small glacier/snowfield, then climbs unusually solid rock up Swiss's southwest face to the broad NW–SE summit ridge; an alternate class 3 line ascends the south side directly from Pickell Pass, and parties approaching from the north describe an 'easy way up' from the Spectre Plateau.
beta: Most ascents happen mid-traverse on the Northern Pickets high route (Luna–East Fury–West Fury–Swiss–Spectre Plateau–Phantom–Ghost–Challenger), first strung together as a continuous crest traverse by Wayne Wallace and Josh Kaplan in 2005 (VI 5.7 overall for the traverse, though Swiss itself is comparatively easy 3rd/4th-class terrain). From a camp near West Fury, cross a short glacier/permanent snowfield northwest of West Fury to the Swiss–Fury saddle, then climb the southwest face on notably sol
breakdown: Approach to saddle: Class 2-3 talus, snow/glacier travel
South Side (alternate, from Pickell Pass): Class 3

first_pass.evidence: Climbed from the snowfield on its southwest side up pleasantly solid rock on the SW face; no class rating found beyond the record's 3rd class.

route: West Ridge / West Face (via Boiling Lake)
overview: A less-traveled alternate line up Switchback's west side, approached via the Boiling Lake basin and the talus benches below Martin Peak, reaching the summit via a boot path on the west face or the class 2-3 west ridge.
beta: An alternate to the Southeast Ridge standard route: from the Boiling Lake area, a way trail contours below Martin and Switchback Peaks at roughly 7,200-7,300 ft; from there, climbers either pick up a boot path up the west face or climb the west ridge proper (class 2-3) to the summit. It sees far less traffic than the Cooney Lake/Southeast Ridge approach and is more commonly used by parties already in the Boiling Lake/Martin Peak basin as part of a larger Sawtooth Ridge traverse.

first_pass.evidence: Approach via Boiling Lake; summit from the west by easy terrain; record gives class 2-3 for the west ridge and no source rates it higher or lower.
Only general references to ice on Table Mountain's East Face found; no route-specific grade beyond the record's WI2 Steep Snow.

overview: Tailgunner (~5,839 ft, also listed as 5,842 ft on older USGS-derived sources) is a minor summit on the rugged ridge linking Gunn Peak and Wing Peak above Barclay Lake, in the Wild Sky Wilderness of the Skykomish Mountains. Gunn Peak, the range highpoint at 6,244 ft, sits just northwest; Baring Mountain rises across the valley to the south. The peak is trail-less and rarely climbed alone — most parties tag it as a side trip from Gunn Peak or Wing Peak via Tailgunner Pass.
beta: From Barclay Lake Trailhead, follow Barclay Creek Trail then leave it to climb the Tailgunner Creek drainage/couloir to Tailgunner Pass (~5,320 ft), a broad saddle between Gunn Peak's ridge and Tailgunner. From the pass, scramble up Tailgunner's west ridge and south-facing scree/rock slopes to the summit dome; a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers. first_pass.evidence: Summer reports call Tailgunner a short, simple scramble; early season via the north slope and a relic-cornice headwall on the west ridge.

face: North face traverse to West/Northwest Ridge
fa: Ed Cooper and Glen Denny, September 9, 1961
overview: A new route rather than the peak's first ascent, climbed in 1961 by Ed Cooper and Glen Denny, ascending to the base of the north ridge, diagonally traversing the northwest face, and topping out via the west ridge. A 2008 party described a similar line as starting up the NE Ridge before an exposed class-4 traverse across the north face gains the NW ridge for an easy class-3 finish.
beta: The 1961 first-ascent party climbed to the base of the north ridge, crossed the northwest face on a diagonal, and finished up the west ridge to the summit. In 2008 the line went as a 3rd-class scramble partway up the NE Ridge, then an exposed traverse across the north face on class-4 ledges, followed by an easy class-3 scramble up the remainder of the NW ridge to the top — tricky route-finding on the north-face ledges is the main technical difficulty.

first_pass.evidence: No route-specific source found for the 1961 Cooper-Denny north/northwest line; record gives exposed Class 4.
